passage: I am Zeenat, and I used to think feedback meant pointing at what was wrong, loudly, so nobody could miss it. In our second year, I led the design team for the college fest, and Dilnaz kept sending posters with the text too small to read from the stage. Once I said so in the group call, in front of eleven people. She went quiet and her posters got worse. Later I messaged her privately. I said the colours were lovely, that the date line was hard to read from the back row, and asked if she'd try a bigger size. She sent a new version that evening. Same work, same me. What changed was where and how I said it. I'm still learning that part, honestly.

qa.q: How many people were on the group call when Zeenat criticised the posters?
qa.a: There were eleven people on the group call.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz probably feeling after being corrected in front of everyone?
qa.a: She was probably embarrassed and defensive, which fits her going quiet and sending worse posters, though she may also have simply been discouraged about the work.

qa.q: What could Zeenat do differently the next time a poster is not readable?
qa.a: She could tell the person privately soon after, name the specific problem such as the small date line, and suggest a fix.

qa.q: How might Zeenat see the public correction now?
qa.a: Zeenat seems a little regretful, seeing that saying it in front of eleven people made things worse while the same feedback worked in private.

grounding: Zeenat recounts a public rebuke that produced defensiveness and a private, specific note that worked.

passage: I was at the next desk in the library when Jomon leaned over to Avni and spoke quietly. I couldn't hear all of it, but I saw him hold up her draft and point at one paragraph. He said something about the second example being unclear, then slid a sticky note across with a suggestion written on it. Avni read it, tucked her hair behind her ear and nodded. Ten minutes later she was typing again, and at one point she laughed and showed him her screen. I don't know what either of them was really thinking. She might have been secretly hurt. But she stayed and worked with him, and he didn't seem to be showing off. Compared with last month, when someone shouted at her over the whole lab, it looked easier to take in. 🙂

qa.q: What did Jomon slide across to Avni?
qa.a: He slid a sticky note with a suggestion written on it.

qa.q: What might Avni have been feeling as she read the note, and what else could it have been?
qa.a: She was most likely receptive, since she nodded and started typing again, but the observer admits she might have been secretly hurt.

qa.q: What made Jomon's way of giving feedback easier to take?
qa.a: He spoke quietly, pointed to one paragraph, and offered a written suggestion, so the feedback was private, specific and usable.

qa.q: How does the observer's view of the two situations differ?
qa.a: The observer sees the quiet desk-side feedback as easier for Avni to absorb than the shouting she got in the lab last month, though they only guess at her inner state.

grounding: An observer describes specific, private, respectful feedback between peers and its calmer reception.
